lesson.title: Photocopying a Gene: The Polymerase Chain Reaction
lesson.summary: PCR, the polymerase chain reaction, amplifies one specific segment of DNA exponentially through repeated cycles of heating and cooling, turning a trace amount of starting material into billions of copies.
lesson.body:
Researchers frequently have only a tiny amount of DNA to work with, a drop of blood at a crime scene, a fragment of ancient bone, a single patient sample, and that tiny amount is not enough to sequence, analyze, or clone directly. PCR solves this problem by essentially running the cell's own DNA replication process inside a test tube, over and over, but focused on copying just one specific stretch of the genome rather than the whole thing, borrowing directly from the natural biology of DNA replication and DNA polymerase covered earlier.

A PCR reaction needs a handful of ingredients: template DNA containing the target region, two primers, which are short synthetic single strands of DNA designed to be complementary to the sequences flanking each end of the target on opposite strands, a heat-stable DNA polymerase, most famously Taq polymerase, originally isolated from Thermus aquaticus, a bacterium that lives in hot springs and whose enzymes evolved to keep working at high temperatures that would destroy an ordinary polymerase, and a supply of the four nucleotide building blocks needed to build new DNA strands.

Each PCR cycle runs through three temperature steps, and each step has a specific job. Denaturation, around 94 to 96 degrees Celsius, uses heat to break the hydrogen bonds holding the double helix together, separating the DNA into two single strands and exposing the template. Annealing, typically around 50 to 65 degrees Celsius, lowers the temperature enough that the primers can bind to their complementary sequences flanking the target region on each strand. Extension, at about 72 degrees Celsius, raises the temperature to Taq polymerase's optimal working range, where it extends each primer, building a new complementary strand by adding nucleotides in the 5' to 3' direction, exactly as DNA polymerase does during normal cell division.

The power of PCR comes from repeating this three-step cycle again and again in a machine called a thermal cycler, which automates the temperature changes. Each cycle roughly doubles the number of DNA molecules containing the target sequence, so after n cycles the target region has been amplified on the order of 2 to the power of n times. Running a typical 25 to 35 cycles can take a reaction from a single starting template molecule to well over a billion copies in the span of a couple of hours. Once a PCR reaction is finished, the very next thing a researcher usually does is load the product onto a gel, using gel electrophoresis from the previous section, to confirm that only a single fragment of the expected size was produced. That PCR product also very often becomes the starting material, the insert, used in DNA cloning, covered next.
